items.question: How do you understand parameter decomposition as an approach to interpreting what a neural network has learned?
items.object: Parameter decomposition as an approach to neural network interpretability
items.answer:
Well, let's contrast it with activation-based decomposition. In interpretability, typically in the past what we've done is wanted to understand what is going on inside a neural network. We've collected lots of activations of how the network has processed its input data. You've got these intermediate activations and then it spits out an output. What we've typically done is started with the idea that these activations should, in some sense, be involved in different things that the network is doing in order to compute its intelligent output. There's some sort of learned algorithm that the network has learned to exhibit its intelligent behavior. Activation decomposition basically is the idea that we can look at these intermediate activations, piece them apart, and say this part does this and this part does that. By contrast, parameter decomposition is philosophically very similarly motivated, but instead of picking apart the activations the idea here is to pick apart the parameters.

Now, why might you want to look at the parameters? Well, in some sense the thing that we're really interested in is the neural network, and the neural network is not its input data, although it interacts in very special ways with it, but the neural network is in some sense the parameters, the architecture that pieces them together, and the nonlinearities that connect them. It uses all these components to transform the input data into activations and transform those activations until it gets to the output. In some sense, the parameters and the architecture and the nonlinearities are the thing that we really want to understand. They are implementing the algorithm that the network has learned, and the activations in some sense are along for the ride, but they do interact in very particular ways where it's not quite as separable as that.

The basic idea here, then, is that the network is using its parameters in different ways for different inputs. For an input where there is a cat, it will take these inputs and spit out a cat label, say. For another input, maybe a picture of the Eiffel Tower, it may not use very many of the same parts of the network as it did when looking at a cat. So, in some sense, there's this idea of modularity. Parts of the network are doing one thing, other parts of the network are doing some other thing. There's a specialization in what the parameters are doing. The aim for parameter decomposition is to find these modules that are doing specific jobs, specific computations. The term that we're looking for here is the mechanisms that the network is using in order to compute its behavior.

To flesh out that cat example a little bit more and to say some really basic stuff: all these neural networks are composed of layers. Often the layers are the same exact structure repeated over and over again, although not always. We've observed by doing interpretability on the activations that we can see things like fur has been detected, eyes have been detected, and a tail has been detected, and we sort of see this gradual move from low-level features to higher-order features as we go through the layers. There's this story of understanding that kind of mirrors, especially in these visual cases, what I understand to also be happening in the human visual system.

items.question: Why do you think identifying concepts in a neural network's activations is insufficient to establish which variables the network actually uses?
items.object: Computations as the basis for identifying which variables a neural network actually uses
items.answer: It gets somewhat philosophical. However, I'll try to convey kind of how I think about this. We can go in and say, look, there's this set of activations, and this set of activations seems to correspond to data points on which there are cats. But maybe we can also find groups of inputs where there's a cat, but it's a cat standing in a particular position. One group of inputs is a cat standing in one position and another in another position. Now, does the network use the fact that there are two different positions of these cats, or does it just have a cat variable? What would it mean to distinguish between a network that just has a cat variable and a network that has multiple different cat variables? My proposition here is that what it means for a network to use particular variables is that these are the variables that the network does its computations over. Now, it may be the case that this network that had multiple cat-in-different-positions variables actually might not use those things. To the network, they're all just cats. But you may nevertheless be able to look really in detail at the data set and find lots of little distinctions within the activations, but the network might not itself actually use these. In some sense we want some way to identify the set of things that the network is using. To do this, you might say, well, this is putting computations first and representations second, rather than putting representations first and then computations second. It's like saying the fundamental variables that the network is using are those over which it does computation. We can maybe find things that the network seems to represent, but there's not a particular reason to say that this is a feature that the network uses just because we can find it in there.

items.question: Why do you think computations are the right starting point for understanding multidimensional and multilayer features in neural networks?
items.object: Computations as the starting point for understanding multidimensional and multilayer neural network features
items.answer:
Since some of the earlier SAE work in the latest bout of sparse coding work in the deep learning space, which maybe started late 2022 and picked up in 2023, some of the observations that people had were things like: it looks like the representations that we're finding seem to be spread across multiple different layers, and it's kind of confusing to think about what that might mean. There were also observations that these things that we were finding were directions in activation space. They're particular patterns of neural activation, but that didn't seem to be the whole story. There seemed to be some sort of multidimensionality to them. It wasn't just one direction. It was perhaps a plane of directions or even higher-dimensional spaces potentially. It was kind of unclear how to think about these higher-dimensional features, so to speak.

Several of the reasons that motivated some of the thinking that led to attribution-based parameter decomposition were: what if a multidimensional feature just is an input variable to a multidimensional computation, and that's indeed why the network has bothered to go to the length to structure its representations in this way? Without there being some sort of multidimensional computation applied to it, you might ask, why did the network bother to structure its activations in this really ordered way? There must be something for which it is using that order. This was why we were thinking maybe it's the computations that are defining the structure of these features, and maybe the same kind of thing might apply in the multilayer case.

For certain networks like transformers, which use a residual stream, it's very easy for computations to be spread over multiple layers because it just works out straightforwardly for them to do this. It was kind of confusing to think about this in terms of SAEs as well. It made some natural sense to think, well, maybe it's the same feature if it interacts with a part of the parameter vector that happens to span multiple layers. For this kind of edge case, this multilayer edge case, it just made a bit more sense to think about the computations rather than representations as primal.

An example is the days of the week, or I think the original grokking result with modular addition would probably fall under this heading. It could vary across different networks, but at least in some settings it has been found that it's not like there are seven days-of-the-week features that light up independently, a strong Monday signal or Tuesday signal. Rather, there seems to be a plane in space through which the day of the week kind of rotates. Remarkably, it seems to crystallize into this—the graphics on this are pretty amazing sometimes—where it's pretty much divided the circle into seven equal shares, and each day of the week has a different direction in this plane, as opposed to each of them having their own independent linear directions. I think the same mechanism, or a similar structure if not the same mechanism, has been found in the grokking result, where to do modular addition things are first translated to an angle, then the angles are added trigonometrically, and then the result of that trigonometric calculation gets mapped back onto the final number.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between parameter decomposition and SAE-based interpretability through the example of days-of-the-week representations?
items.object: Parameter decomposition versus SAE-based interpretability
items.answer:
I think it's probably easiest to think about the days-of-the-week case. To be clear, it can be both that there is a multidimensional aspect to these representations as well as individual days aspects to these representations. The reason is that sometimes you might want to, in some tasks, say, well, the day after Tuesday is—and you might just apply the computation that rotates the day-of-the-week feature, because now you've just got one mechanism that you can apply to every single day of the week. But in some settings you might really just want one day. You might just say, “I was on my way to the shop on…” and there's really just one direction that you want to say here, say it's Monday. So in some settings you may just want computations that apply to these individual days, and some settings where you might want this higher-dimensional computation, this two-dimensional one that might rotate it.

This is an important aspect of parameter decomposition: not one basis that you might use to interpret the whole model. There are steps in an algorithm, and sometimes these steps will be useful and others will not. The SAE approach might not find this shared computation that just rotates from one day to the next. It might find, conditioned on prompts that say “the day after” or “the following day,” one for Tuesday, one for Wednesday, one for Thursday, just to rotate around every single time. This is because it's trying to find sparsely activating parts of the data set that have a particular shared property, and in particular parts of the data set that have a particular shared direction in activation space, which is not necessarily all the ways in which inputs might share properties. One of the ways they might share properties is they use similar mechanisms, and these mechanisms may do the same operation but to different inputs depending on what the prompt is.

I'm not sure if that was clear, but this is one of the differences you might expect from parameter decomposition and an SAE-like approach. There are other approaches that might get closer to what you might expect or want to find with an approach that identifies the computations. For instance, Anthropic recently released an update on “multimodal...” I will need to remind myself what that stands for, but there's a similar principle here where instead of looking at individual directions, it's looking at more multidimensional computations.

items.question: What do you see as a potential blind spot of SAE approaches to interpreting neural networks as those networks become more powerful?
items.object: Potential blind spots of SAE approaches as neural networks become more powerful
items.answer: I think a key point is functions that are reused on different inputs and do the same semantically meaningful transformation on a given input. That is something that the SAE approach could be entirely blind to, but which obviously is a pretty important aspect and potentially happens a whole lot. We don't really know yet how much that may happen, but certainly seems like it probably should happen a lot, right? Especially as we get to more and more powerful networks, it would seem like we are moving away from, or graduating perhaps in a sense from, simple rule-based combinations of distinct features and probably toward higher and higher-level abstractions, which would presumably then correspond to more functions that can operate over ranges of inputs and do the same useful transformation to some space of inputs.

items.question: Why do you think parameter decomposition could capture simple neural-network transformations more naturally than an SAE or a transcoder?
items.object: Representing simple neural-network transformations with SAEs, transcoders, and parameter decomposition
items.answer: I think one of the cases that I like to think about is in an SAE, or a transcoder, which is an SAE that takes as input some activation and spits out a prediction of what the activation will be at the next layer. Both of these will have a problem where suppose the network is just doing a simple transformation. Suppose it's a rotation or suppose indeed that it's actually just an identity transformation. You're going to have to spend a lot of representational capacity to represent the computations that the network is doing at this particular transformation. Why? Because you've got, say, a million different features, and there's a million different features in the output, especially in the case of the identity transformation. There are going to be a million there, and you would need one input feature and one output feature for each input-output pair, whereas in essence what the network is doing is actually very simple. It's just a transformation of this type, whether it's an identity or a rotation, and you've just got one object doing that transformation. That's the kind of thing that we want parameter decomposition to be able to find, if it is indeed the case that networks are doing that kind of thing.

items.question: How do you think neural networks can carry out more computations than they have neurons?
items.object: Computational superposition in neural networks
items.answer: We think that there are many different computations going on inside this network, more indeed than it has neurons. The way we think networks can do this is that they spread their computations out over their computational units, the neurons. By spreading it out, you get some nice properties, such as avoiding—even though you might overlap with other computations—noise that comes from this overlap. You can basically fit more in because you're silencing the stuff that you don't really want to be there, the kind of computations you don't really want to be active right now. It's very similar principles to the idea of representation and superposition, but brought into computational space.

The way we think networks can do this is that they spread their computations out over their computational units, the neurons. By spreading it out, you get some nice properties, such as avoiding—even though you might overlap with other computations—noise that comes from this overlap. You don't necessarily need to; you can basically fit more in because you're silencing the stuff that you don't really want to be there, the kind of computations you don't really want to be active right now. items.question: How do you understand model unmerging as a way to separate the computations inside a neural network?
items.object: Model unmerging as a way to separate neural-network computations
items.answer: There's this extra layer to what the network is doing. We've split it out into this extra dimension where you're asking what computations the network is using at this particular layer and in this particular width dimension as well. This does have precedent in other areas of deep learning. Mixture of experts might be an example of this, where you have layers, you have individual networks, but you can do different computations at the same neuron dimension, so to speak, depending on which expert you use. There are senses in which this is like, well, suppose every single network is just a big mixture of experts that's been smushed together. Can we separate out the experts? items.question: Why do you use a learned causal importance function in stochastic parameter decomposition instead of keeping only the top-k parameter components?

items.answer:

The way we did that was we literally turned them off and only kept on the top-k parameter components. What this is really saying is it shouldn't matter if this parameter component is on or off. It could be on to its full extent, off to its full extent, or anywhere in between, and it really should not affect the output. The top-k approach was not great at optimizing this, such that if you did turn it on a little amount, it probably still would do stuff.

What we're basically doing in stochastic parameter decomposition is learning a function that predicts, for a given input, how ablatable, how turn-offable, this subcomponent is. If it is turn-offable, it shouldn't matter how much we turn it off by; it's causally irrelevant. We have this causal importance function that predicts one number, the causal importance value for this subcomponent on this data point. It's supposed to be between zero and one. To the extent that it is zero, we can randomly mask this subcomponent on this input anywhere between zero and one; that is to say, we can turn it on randomly anywhere between zero and one. If this causal importance value is one, we don't get to randomly modify or mask it at all. It has to be on because it's really causally important. We literally have a neural network that spits out this one number for each subcomponent. If the subcomponent is very causally important and it gets the right causal importance value of one, great. But if it is causally important and the network accidentally spits out 0.5, then this parameter subcomponent can be masked anywhere between one and 0.5. If it's masked anywhere that's not one, along this random distribution, it's going to damage the loss. This means gradients will be able to flow into this causal importance function that produced this number, using the reparameterization trick to pass gradients through this random sample and output this random distribution. It learns to approximate how ablatable this parameter component is for a given input.

items.question: How do you think about the architectural complexity needed for the causal importance function in your parameter decomposition method?

items.question: Why do you find stochastic parameter decomposition a better algorithm to work with than attribution-based parameter decomposition?
items.object: Stochastic parameter decomposition compared with attribution-based parameter decomposition
items.answer:
I think it might also be time to revisit the garbage component. We were talking about a case where maybe the network has learned these subcomponents, and maybe they're actually doing a slightly different algorithm from the original network. In APD, you could switch them off and never activate them. You can kind of compensate for one component that's active doing a different thing while still summing up to the parameters of the original network. In stochastic parameter decomposition, you can't really do that anymore because you're randomly activating every part of the network basically all the time. If it's doing something it shouldn't be doing, it's going to modify the activations in a way that the original network didn't, and that's going to be bad for the loss.

It's important to realize that we're not actually able to turn off subcomponents in SPD. There are no dead components or anything. What it means for it to be a dead component is not that you never activate it, but that you activate it randomly all the time. I think this is fundamentally different from being completely silenced all the time, and gets rid of a lot of pathologies like the one you mentioned. It also gets around the discontinuity in the top-k optimization, where you're only activating the top-k and the rest are silent. If you're silenced, gradients aren't really flowing through you. Your parameters can't really learn to be better. Whereas, if you're always on randomly all the time, gradients are always flowing through every subcomponent. It feels like there's a lot more continuity in the learning process.

This pans out in that the algorithm is still somewhat sensitive to getting hyperparameters right. However, in attribution-based parameter decomposition it was not only sensitive, it was not well behaved. You'd change something one way and it changed unpredictably. In stochastic parameter decomposition, there's a range in which you need your hyperparameters to exist, but because things are well behaved, you can find them without having to guess what to change. It's much nicer to work with than the previous algorithm.

That said, the method we introduced in the paper is not perfect. Since publishing, we've focused on changing things and found better versions for sampling the randomness and the gates we used in the causal importance functions, to make it a better-behaved algorithm overall. There's still optimization on algorithms to do, but it's significantly better to work with than the previous method, which makes us excited for scaling this up to larger models. We've begun to do that for small transformers, including language models.

items.question: Why do you think increasingly fine-grained features in sparse autoencoders can make a neural network less interpretable?
items.object: Feature splitting in sparse autoencoders (SAEs)
items.answer:
We've talked already about one of the examples with the cat and the cat in a number of different positions, and it's not clear whether or not the network is actually using these more fine-grained features that you can identify. From a practical point of view, we don't want our explanations to explain more than they need to. We can explain how the network takes one of these cats in one position and applies circuits to it, and do it for the next cat in another position, and so on, but we're wasting our time if the network isn't really using these variables in its algorithms. We want to avoid doing unnecessary explanation. We want our descriptions of what the network is doing to be minimal in some sense.

Another particularly pathological case of SAE feature splitting is feature absorption. You might have, in one smaller SAE, a feature for words that begin with the letter E. In a larger SAE with more fine-grained features, you have a feature for elephant and a feature for everything else that begins with the letter E, or it splits into other words that begin with E. In some sense, this other decomposition, the one with more features, is less interpretable because there was no need for us to split out elephant. Maybe we just want the variables on which the network is working. There's no obvious way to avoid this using SAEs.

There may be a perfect stopping point for SAEs, such that beyond this point you're using variables that the network is using, and before that you're not. There may be a point at which you go into a regime where you've got SAE features that are the corresponding variables that the network is not using, and before that you've got only variables that the network is using. But that's not obvious either. You could find these sparsely activating directions in activation space, but there's no guaranteed reason to expect that these are the way in which the network is chunking up its computations. Maybe it's a group of SAE features that the network is actually using, and maybe you needed to split further for this group. There's no guaranteed reason that SAE features will find variables for computations.

items.question: How do you judge what level of granularity makes sense when decomposing a neural network into components?
items.object: Choosing the granularity of a neural network decomposition
items.answer:
Whenever we're optimizing these things and saying this is the right decomposition, there's an asterisk. We're saying this is for a given amount of decomposition. This is the decomposition that breaks it up into as few components as are necessary to explain a given level of functionality of the network. We can scale up and down the amount of decomposition we want to do and break up the network into larger or smaller parts.
There's some reason to prefer some regions of this spectrum over others. One reason might be that the reconstruction loss, as you scale and decompose things more and more, gets a lot worse. Correspondingly, there may be a point where your causal importances, these values that are supposed to tell us how important each subcomponent is, behave pathologically. For instance, they might all typically take fractional values rather than values that should be one or zero. If something's causally important, it can be partly causally important, which will shed light on how much loss we might lose by ablating it. But by and large, we prefer regimes where it's a bit more binary. There are points along this spectrum, as we modify hyperparameters that control how much decomposition or activation sparsity is going on, that give us clues as to what decompositions make sense.

items.question: How do you think about the possibility of finding a single ground-truth decomposition of a neural network?
items.object: The possibility of a ground-truth neural network decomposition
items.answer: In some sense, none of these decompositions are right. This holds true for sparse dictionary learning and parameter decomposition. We're dealing with one fundamental truth, the original network, and we're trying to get a lens on what it is doing under the hood. None of our lenses are going to be perfect. They're always going to introduce approximations of some sort. This is a necessity. We're trying to discretize a fundamentally continuous object in various ways. Whenever you do that, you're going to throw out some nonzero amount of approximation quality. We're willing to pay these costs to get tractable explanations, even though there is not one actual ground-truth decomposition.

items.question: What advantages do you see in parameter decomposition for unlearning and monitoring compared with sparse autoencoders?
items.object: Parameter decomposition for unlearning and monitoring
items.answer: I think it should make unlearning more straightforward than in SAEs, because you're already working in parameter space. You already know this is the direction that does X, and we can modify this vector in parameter space. We have a more straightforward lens onto functions as they relate to parameter space. Whether or not this beats some gradient-descent-guided approach is a separate question, but I think monitoring is also something that it will be useful for, to the same or greater extent than sparse autoencoders or other approaches. Sparse autoencoders might be detecting a particular region of the training dataset. Perhaps it's too narrow a region. Instead, what we really wanted was whenever the network was using function X, that's when we want to pay more attention and go into detail on what it's doing, rather than whether there was an activation in this particular direction. There's going to be some correlation between these. There will be things we want to monitor that might be better thought of in terms of functions. To get less abstract, maybe there's a function for deception, and there are many different situations in which a model might be doing deception. The input directions might be different, and the intermediate computations might point in different directions in a way that SAEs might struggle to identify as the one direction that does deception. It may instead have many different directions that do this. In stochastic parameter decomposition and later versions of this approach, we hope to identify the individual components that are doing this functionality.
